screens.title: Logical Volume Management (LVM)
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how LVM gives you a flexible layer over physical disks so you can grow, shrink, snapshot, and move storage without the rigidity of traditional partitions. LVM is built from three layers: physical volumes which wrap disks or partitions, volume groups which pool those disks, and logical volumes which you format and mount like partitions. Practically, you'll create PVs, assemble them into a VG, carve LVs, and then format and mount them. We will demonstrate the key commands used in day-to-day administration and show the correct order of operations for extending and for reducing space. A critical part of this lesson is safety: when shrinking, shrink the filesystem first, always have backups, and know that some filesystems cannot be reduced. You will also see how snapshots let you make point-in-time copies useful for backups and testing. By the end of the module you should be able to build an LVM-backed volume from two raw disks, extend an LV while the service is running, and choose a safe migration path when shrinking is required. Consider this a practical toolkit for managing live servers with minimal disruption.

Logical Volume Management (LVM)

Use LVM to pool disks, carve flexible volumes, grow storage online, and create snapshots for safe backups and testing.

In this lesson

You will initialize disks as PVs, build a VG, create LVs, format and mount them, then safely extend and snapshot volumes on a live system.

Why this matters

Rigid partitions make life hard. LVM lets you add capacity, move data, and protect snapshots without long downtime, which is essential for production servers.

Safety note

When reducing storage, always shrink the filesystem before lvreduce and verify backups. Some filesystems, like XFS, cannot be shrunk.

screens.title: LVM components: PV, VG, LV
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the three core components of LVM and build a clear mental model. A Physical Volume, or PV, is the raw storage device or partition that LVM initializes and uses. It maps to a disk or partition like a whole extra disk or a single partition flagged for LVM. A Volume Group, VG, is a pool composed of one or more PVs; think of it as a single large virtual disk that aggregates capacity. Logical Volumes, LVs, are carved from the VG and are what you format with a filesystem and mount into the directory tree. A strong mental model: PVs are the bricks, the VG is the storage silo, and LVs are the containers you cut out to hold data. A practical example: if you add two 10 GB disks as PVs to a VG, that VG will present roughly 20 GB of pool space from which you can create multiple LVs of varying sizes. A common misconception is to treat an LV as a fixed partition; in reality you can extend or shrink an LV within the space available in its VG. Remember, changes to LVs are quick, but filesystem changes must be handled correctly. A takeaway: understand the layered roles and how they let you treat many physical devices as one flexible logical resource.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › LVM components
Definition

PV, VG, LV explained

PVs are disks or partitions initialized for LVM. VGs pool multiple PVs into a single resource. LVs are allocated from the VG and formatted with filesystems for mounting.

Analogy: Bricks, Silo, Containers

PVs are bricks, VG is the silo that stores capacity, and LVs are the containers you take from the silo to store data.

Concrete example

Two 1GB disks as PVs make a 2GB VG. From that VG you can create a 1.5GB LV for application data and a 400MB LV for logs.

Common misconception

An LV is not a fixed partition. You can extend its size if the VG has free space; but remember filesystem resizing is a separate step.

Command reference
# Initialize two partitions as physical volumes
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Create a volume group named my_vg from those PVs
sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Create a 1.5G logical volume named my_lv in my_vg
sudo lvcreate -L 1.5G -n my_lv my_vg

# Format and mount
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo mkdir -p /lvmdata
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv /lvmdata
Key Takeaway

Think in layers: prepare disks (PVs), pool them (VG), and carve flexible volumes (LV) for filesystems and mounts.

screens.title: Initializing Physical Volumes
screens.narratorSegment: Before LVM can use a disk, the device must be prepared as a physical volume. Typically you will create a single partition on each raw disk and set its type to Linux LVM where applicable. This is often done with a partitioning tool, but the essential LVM step is pvcreate which writes LVM metadata to the device so it can be combined later. A practical example: after partitioning two disks as /dev/sdb1 and /dev/sdc1, run pvcreate on both devices. Verify success with pvs or pvdisplay to confirm the LVM label and available space. A common operational pitfall is running pvcreate on a disk that contains data; pvcreate will overwrite partition metadata, so only initialize disks that are new or intentionally cleared. Another tip: use partprobe or reboot if the kernel doesn't see new partitions yet. After you have created PVs, you can combine them into a volume group. The core command sequence is simple, but verification and caution are essential. Ask yourself before pvcreate: is the device empty or backed up? Initializing Physical Volumes means pvcreate writes lvm metadata to a disk or partition; verify with pvs and ensure the device contains no needed data before initializing.. In practical terms, preparing raw disks or partitions for lvm use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Initializing PVs
Definition

Prepare disks with pvcreate

Use pvcreate to initialize a disk or partition for LVM; this writes essential metadata so the device can join a VG.

Step-by-step
  1. Partition the disk with a single partition type for LVM (optional but recommended).
  2. Run pvcreate on the partition or disk.
  3. Verify with pvs or pvdisplay.
Danger

pvcreate overwrites existing metadata. Do not run it on disks with live data unless you have a verified backup.

Terminal demo
# Partition disks (optional)
sudo gdisk /dev/sdb    # create single partition type 8e00
sudo gdisk /dev/sdc    # create single partition type 8e00
sudo partprobe

# Initialize physical volumes
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Verify
sudo pvs
# or
sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb1
Key Takeaway

Partition carefully, run pvcreate only on disks you intend for LVM, and always verify with pvs or pvdisplay.

screens.title: Building a Volume Group and adding PVs
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have initialized one or more PVs, the next step is to assemble them into a volume group. Use vgcreate to make a VG from the PVs and give it a meaningful name. For example, creating my_vg from two PVs combines their capacity into a single pool. Later, if you add more disks, you can add PVs to the VG with vgextend without downtime for existing LVs. Verify the VG name and free space with vgs or vgdisplay. A practical tip: choose VG names that reflect purpose, such as data_vg or db_vg, to avoid confusion. A common misconception is that adding a PV automatically grows LVs; it only increases pool capacity; you must still extend an LV explicitly. Another pitfall is attempting to remove a PV while it still contains extents used by LVs; vgreduce is required to remove PVs from a VG after migrating data off them with pvmove. The safe workflow is: create VG, monitor free extents, extend VG as needed, then extend or create LVs to consume that free space. Building a Volume Group and adding PVs means vgcreate makes a pool from pvs; vgextend adds capacity later. lvs consume space from the vg but do not grow automatically.. In practical terms, create a vg and extend it when capacity grows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Volume Groups
Quick steps

Create and extend a VG

Use vgcreate to make a volume group and vgextend to add more physical volumes later. Monitor free space with vgs or vgdisplay.

Example

Create my_vg from /dev/sdb1 and /dev/sdc1, then add /dev/sdd1 later with vgextend.

Misconception

Adding PVs increases the pool but does not change existing LV sizes automatically. You must run lvextend to grow an LV.

Terminal commands
# Create a volume group
sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1

# Add a new physical volume later
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd1
sudo vgextend my_vg /dev/sdd1

# Verify
sudo vgs
sudo vgdisplay my_vg
Key Takeaway

VGs aggregate PV capacity. Extend the VG to add pool space, then extend LVs to increase usable storage.

screens.title: Create and mount a Logical Volume
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a logical volume is the point where storage becomes usable by services. After you have a VG, use lvcreate to allocate an LV with a name and size. The LV becomes a block device under /dev/your_vg/your_lv. Next, format that device with a filesystem command such as mkfs. ext4 and mount it to a directory. This sequence is common in server provisioning: create LV, format, create mount point, and mount. Verify the mount and space with df -h. A practical example is creating a 1.5 gigabyte LV named my_lv in my_vg, formatting it with ext4, then mounting it at /lvmdata. A common mistake is creating the LV but forgetting to resize the filesystem after extending; the OS will not see new usable space until the filesystem itself is resized. Another operational note: set appropriate ownership and permissions on the mount point for the service using it. Finally, record the mount in /etc/fstab if you want it to persist across reboots, using the block device path or a UUID. Always verify with df -h and lvs after each step. Create and mount a Logical Volume means lvcreate allocates the logical device, mkfs formats it, and mount makes it available. verify with lvs and df -h.. In practical terms, lvcreate, mkfs, and mount — the full workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Create & Mount LV
Task

Create an LV and mount it

Allocate storage for an application by creating an LV, formatting it, and mounting it at an application path.

Concrete example

Create a 1.5G LV named my_lv in my_vg, mkfs.ext4 it, mount at /lvmdata, and check space with df -h.

Pro tip

Record the LV in /etc/fstab if the device path or UUID should mount after reboot. Use mount by UUID for stability.

Commands (terminal-style)
# Create LV
sudo lvcreate -L 1.5G -n my_lv my_vg

# Format and mount
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo mkdir -p /lvmdata
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv /lvmdata

# Verify
df -h /lvmdata
sudo lvs
Key Takeaway

An LV is a block device. Format and mount it just like a partition, and verify with lvs and df -h.

screens.title: Inspecting LVM: pvs, vgs, lvs
screens.narratorSegment: Inspecting LVM state is a routine and essential task. The pvs, vgs, and lvs commands provide quick, human-friendly summaries of physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes respectively. pvdisplay, vgdisplay, and lvdisplay offer verbose output with detailed metadata. Use these commands to check free space, VG names, LV paths, and attributes before making changes. For example, before extending an LV, run vgs to confirm the VG has free extents. After extending and resizing, run lvs and df -h to verify both the logical device and the filesystem reflect the new capacity. A common error is trusting one tool alone; cross-check with df -h to confirm the filesystem size and with lvs to confirm logical device size. Another useful trick is running commands with the -o option to customize output columns for scripts and automation. Regularly using these commands helps avoid mistakes such as removing a PV that still holds extents or assuming an LV is unmounted when it is not. Inspecting LVM: pvs, vgs, lvs means use pvs/vgs/lvs and pvdisplay/vgdisplay/lvdisplay to verify allocation and free space before and after operations.. In practical terms, use inspection commands to confirm state and capacity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Inspecting LVM
Command comparison

pvs vs vgs vs lvs

Use pvs to see physical volumes and free extents, vgs to inspect pooled capacity, and lvs to inspect logical volumes and their sizes and attributes.

  • pvs: quick PV summary; pvdisplay for details.
  • vgs: shows VG free space and extent sizes; vgdisplay for details.
  • lvs: shows LV sizes, paths, and attributes; lvdisplay for metadata.
Terminal examples
# Quick summaries
sudo pvs
sudo vgs
sudo lvs

# Verbose details
sudo pvdisplay /dev/sdb1
sudo vgdisplay my_vg
sudo lvdisplay /dev/my_vg/my_lv

# Use df -h to confirm filesystem size
df -h /lvmdata
Check before change

Always confirm free extents in the VG and that the target LV is unmounted or quiesced before destructive operations.

screens.title: Extending Logical Volumes and filesystems
screens.narratorSegment: Extending storage is one of LVM's biggest advantages. The safe sequence is to extend the logical volume, then resize the filesystem so the OS can use the new space. For ext4 systems you can usually run resize2fs while the filesystem is mounted; for XFS you must use xfs_growfs and specify the mount point. A typical example: if your LV needs 10 more gigabytes and the VG has free space, run lvextend with +10G to grow the LV, then run resize2fs on the LV block device or on the mount point if using ext4. Verify with df -h to see the increased capacity. A common error is to extend the LV but forget to resize the filesystem, leaving the extra space unusable. Another consideration is to prefer growing in logical extents or with +100%FREE when you want to consume all available pool space. Always verify the VG free space before attempting an lvextend. If multiple services rely on the filesystem, plan short maintenance or use online resize capabilities carefully. Extending Logical Volumes and filesystems means use lvextend to increase the block device and resize2fs or xfs_growfs to update the filesystem so it can use the added space.. In practical terms, lvextend then resize the filesystem to make space usable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: Extending storage is one of LVM's biggest advantages. The safe sequence is to extend the logical volume, then resize the filesystem so the OS can use the new space. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Extending LVs
How to

lvextend and resize the FS

Extend the LV to grow the underlying block device, then run the appropriate filesystem resize tool so the OS can use the new blocks.

Example sequence

Extend by 5GB, then resize the ext4 filesystem to use the added space, then confirm with df -h.

Common mistake

Forgetting the filesystem resize step means the LV is larger but the filesystem still reports the old capacity.

Commands
# Extend LV by 5GB
sudo lvextend -L +5G /dev/my_vg/my_lv

# For ext4 (device or mount point may be used)
sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/my_lv
# or if mounted
sudo resize2fs /lvmdata

# For XFS (must specify mount point)
sudo xfs_growfs /lvmdata

# Verify
df -h /lvmdata
sudo lvs
Key Takeaway

Extending is a two-step operation: grow the LV, then grow the filesystem. Confirm with lvs and df -h.

screens.title: Resizing ext4 filesystems after growth
screens.narratorSegment: When working with ext4 filesystems, resize2fs is the tool you will use to adjust the filesystem size to match the underlying block device. After running lvextend to increase the LV, resize2fs will expand the filesystem to use the new space. The tool can operate while the filesystem is mounted on many systems, which makes online expansion convenient. A concrete example: after adding five gigabytes to an LV, run resize2fs pointed at the block device or the mount point; both approaches ensure metadata and allocation structures grow properly. Always run df -h to confirm the mount shows the new size and lvs to confirm the LV itself grew. A common misconception is believing a filesystem auto-resizes with the LV; it does not. Another safety check is to run a filesystem check with e2fsck before a reduction operation, but avoid running e2fsck on a mounted filesystem. For reductions, the sequence is the reverse and requires unmounting and explicit checks. The core insight: separate device size from filesystem size and use the right tool for the filesystem type. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Resizing ext4
Definition & Use

Use resize2fs after lvextend

resize2fs updates ext4 metadata to use the newly added space. It is commonly safe to run while mounted for expansion.

Example

After lvextend, run resize2fs on the LV device or the mount point and then verify with df -h.

Shrink caution

Do not use resize2fs to shrink while mounted. For reductions, unmount first and run filesystem checks before shrinking.

Example commands
# After lvextend
sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/my_lv
# Or if preferred for mounted ext4
sudo resize2fs /lvmdata

# Verify
df -h /lvmdata
sudo lvs

# For reduction (high risk): unmount first
sudo umount /lvmdata
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/my_lv 8G
sudo lvreduce -L 9G /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv /lvmdata
Key Takeaway

For ext4, resize2fs makes new space usable. For shrinking, unmount and check the filesystem first to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Reducing Logical Volumes safely
screens.narratorSegment: Shrinking logical volumes is a high-risk operation and requires strict sequencing. The fundamental rule: shrink the filesystem first, then shrink the logical volume. For ext4, that means unmounting the filesystem, running a filesystem check to ensure integrity, resizing the filesystem smaller than the target LV size, and only then performing lvreduce to reduce the LV. Afterward, remount and verify. If you attempt to reduce the LV before shrinking the filesystem, you will corrupt metadata and lose data. For XFS, the situation is different: XFS cannot be shrunk. If you need to reduce an XFS-backed LV, you must either back up data, recreate a smaller filesystem, and restore, or create a new smaller LV and copy data over. This is the common misconception tested in assessments. Always have recent backups before any reduce operation and practice the steps in a lab environment so you can complete them confidently and quickly when under pressure. The safe path is conservative: unmount, e2fsck, resize filesystem, lvreduce, remount, verify. Reducing Logical Volumes safely means always shrink the filesystem first, then the lv. xfs cannot be shrunk — backup-and-restore or copy to a new lv is required.. In practical terms, why shrinking is risky and the correct sequence to avoid data loss. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always shrink the filesystem first, then the LV. XFS cannot be shrunk — backup-and-restore or copy to a new LV is required.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Reducing LVs
Critical safety

Shrink filesystem, then lvreduce

Follow a strict sequence for reductions and always have backups. Treat XFS as immutable for shrink operations.

Danger zone

Shrinking the LV before the filesystem will cause immediate data loss. Never skip filesystem checks before shrink.

XFS caveat

XFS cannot be reduced. Use backup, recreate, and restore, or copy data to a new smaller LV instead of trying to shrink an XFS filesystem.

Safe command sequence (ext4)
# Unmount the filesystem
sudo umount /data

# Check filesystem integrity (ext4)
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/my_vg/my_lv

# Shrink filesystem to a size smaller than target LV
sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/my_lv 8G

# Shrink logical volume (keep it slightly larger than filesystem)
sudo lvreduce -L 9G /dev/my_vg/my_lv

# Remount and verify
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv /data
df -h /data
Key Takeaway

Treat reductions as dangerous operations. Plan backups, follow the shrink-first rule, and avoid attempting to shrink XFS directly.

screens.title: LVM Snapshots
screens.narratorSegment: Snapshots are a powerful LVM feature that lets you capture a point-in-time view of an LV without copying the entire volume. When you create a snapshot, LVM records changes to the original LV and stores only changed blocks in the snapshot volume. This is efficient for short-term backups and testing. A basic example is creating a snapshot named my_lv_snap with a small allocation for changed blocks; mount the snapshot to inspect or copy files as they existed at creation time. Snapshots are not a substitute for backups because they often live on the same physical devices and can fill if too many changes occur. Create snapshots with lvcreate -s and a size that accommodates expected changes. After you finish, remove the snapshot with lvremove to reclaim space. A common misconception is that snapshots are free; they consume space for changes and can influence performance. Use snapshots judiciously and remove them when they are no longer needed. LVM Snapshots means lvcreate -s makes a snapshot that records changed blocks so you can mount a point-in-time copy without duplicating unchanged data.. In practical terms, create and use point-in-time snapshots for backups and testing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › LVM Snapshots
Concept

Point-in-time copies with lvcreate -s

Snapshots capture the state of an LV at creation time by tracking changed blocks. They are efficient but consume space for changes and are not a full backup substitute.

Use cases

Backups, testing upgrades, or taking a safe copy before risky changes.

Caution

Snapshots can fill if the original LV changes extensively; monitor snapshot usage and remove when done.

Example commands
# Create a 200MB snapshot named my_lv_snap
sudo lvcreate -L 200M -s -n my_lv_snap /dev/my_vg/my_lv

# Verify snapshots and LVs
sudo lvs

# Mount the snapshot to inspect
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/my_lv_snap
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv_snap /mnt/my_lv_snap

# When finished, remove snapshot
sudo umount /mnt/my_lv_snap
sudo lvremove /dev/my_vg/my_lv_snap
Key Takeaway

Snapshots are efficient change-tracking copies. They are ideal for short-term testing and backups but must be sized and managed carefully.

keyIdea.text: Partition, pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, mkfs, mount, lvextend, resize2fs, create and remove snapshot — verify after each step.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Hands-on Activity

Guided lab: two-disk LVM build

Follow the commands below in order, verifying after each group with the inspection commands to confirm success.

# (Optional) Partition disks /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc as LVM type
sudo gdisk /dev/sdb
sudo gdisk /dev/sdc
sudo partprobe

# Initialize PVs
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo pvs

# Create VG
sudo vgcreate my_vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo vgs

# Create LV
sudo lvcreate -L 1.5G -n my_lv my_vg
sudo lvs

# Format and mount
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo mkdir -p /lvmdata
sudo mount /dev/my_vg/my_lv /lvmdata
df -h /lvmdata

# Extend LV by 500M and resize filesystem
sudo lvextend -L +500M /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo resize2fs /dev/my_vg/my_lv
df -h /lvmdata

# Create snapshot and then remove it
sudo lvcreate -L 200M -s -n my_lv_snap /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo lvs
sudo umount /lvmdata  # if you mounted snapshot elsewhere, unmount snapshot
sudo lvremove /dev/my_vg/my_lv_snap

# Cleanup (lab tidy)
sudo umount /lvmdata
sudo lvremove /dev/my_vg/my_lv
sudo vgremove my_vg
sudo pvremove /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
Key Takeaway

Perform checks after each command group and keep backups before any destructive step. Practice in a VM until the sequence is smooth.

Lab Warning

This lab modifies disks. Use throwaway virtual disks or snapshots of your VM to avoid accidental data loss.

Second, most LVM tasks are simple sequences of commands: use pvcreate to initialize, vgcreate or vgextend to manage pools, lvcreate and lvextend to allocate and grow logical devices, and format and mount to make them usable. Keep these core concepts top of mind when you plan storage operations on live servers.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how LVM gives you a flexible layer over physical disks so you can grow, shrink, snapshot, and move storage without the rigidity of traditional partitions. LVM is built from three layers: physical volumes which wrap disks or partitions, volume groups which pool those disks, and logical volumes which you format and mount like partitions. Practically, you'll create PVs, assemble them into a VG, carve LVs, and then format and mount them. We will demonstrate the key commands used in day-to-day administration and show the correct order of operations for extending and for reducing space. A critical part of this lesson is safety: when shrinking, shrink the filesystem first, always have backups, and know that some filesystems cannot be reduced. You will also see how snapshots let you make point-in-time copies useful for backups and testing. By the end of the module you should be able to build an LVM-backed volume from two raw disks, extend an LV while the service is running, and choose a safe migration path when shrinking is required. Consider this a practical toolkit for managing live servers with minimal disruption.

These objectives map to practical tasks you will perform on a Linux system. First, you should be able to explain why LVM matters: how it abstracts physical disks into a flexible pool and the roles of PV, VG, and LV. Second, you will create PVs from raw disks, assemble them into a VG, and carve out LVs which you format and mount; this is core hands-on skill for a sysadmin. Third, you will safely extend an LV and the filesystem it holds while minimizing downtime by using the appropriate resize tools. Fourth, you will practice the critical safety path for shrinking volumes and understand snapshots as a non-destructive way to capture a point-in-time copy. Each objective is tied to commands and checks that you will run, and each builds toward verified competency where you can perform the operation reliably on production-like systems.

This second objective slide focuses on applied skills you will practice. You will perform a hands-on sequence: partition raw disks optionally for LVM, initialize them as PVs with pvcreate, and combine them into a VG with vgcreate. Then you will create an LV with lvcreate, format it with a filesystem like ext4, and mount it to a directory so services can use it. You will also practice expanding an LV while a service is running by extending the LV and then resizing the filesystem to consume the new space. Finally, you will create a snapshot and mount it to inspect a point-in-time view of data. Each of these operations will be accompanied by verification commands such as pvs, vgs, lvs, and df so you can confirm the results. The learning path ensures you can repeat the commands reliably in a lab or production environment.

Let's define the three core components of LVM and build a clear mental model. A Physical Volume, or PV, is the raw storage device or partition that LVM initializes and uses. It maps to a disk or partition like a whole extra disk or a single partition flagged for LVM. A Volume Group, VG, is a pool composed of one or more PVs; think of it as a single large virtual disk that aggregates capacity. Logical Volumes, LVs, are carved from the VG and are what you format with a filesystem and mount into the directory tree. A strong mental model: PVs are the bricks, the VG is the storage silo, and LVs are the containers you cut out to hold data. A practical example: if you add two 10 GB disks as PVs to a VG, that VG will present roughly 20 GB of pool space from which you can create multiple LVs of varying sizes. A common misconception is to treat an LV as a fixed partition; in reality you can extend or shrink an LV within the space available in its VG. Remember, changes to LVs are quick, but filesystem changes must be handled correctly. A takeaway: understand the layered roles and how they let you treat many physical devices as one flexible logical resource.

Before LVM can use a disk, the device must be prepared as a physical volume. Typically you will create a single partition on each raw disk and set its type to Linux LVM where applicable. This is often done with a partitioning tool, but the essential LVM step is pvcreate which writes LVM metadata to the device so it can be combined later. A practical example: after partitioning two disks as /dev/sdb1 and /dev/sdc1, run pvcreate on both devices. Verify success with pvs or pvdisplay to confirm the LVM label and available space. A common operational pitfall is running pvcreate on a disk that contains data; pvcreate will overwrite partition metadata, so only initialize disks that are new or intentionally cleared. Another tip: use partprobe or reboot if the kernel doesn't see new partitions yet. After you have created PVs, you can combine them into a volume group. Extending storage is one of LVM's biggest advantages. The safe sequence is to extend the logical volume, then resize the filesystem so the OS can use the new space. Shrinking logical volumes is a high-risk operation and requires strict sequencing. The fundamental rule: shrink the filesystem first, then shrink the logical volume. Snapshots are a powerful LVM feature that lets you capture a point-in-time view of an LV without copying the entire volume. When you create a snapshot, LVM records changes to the original LV and stores only changed blocks in the snapshot volume. This is efficient for short-term backups and testing. A basic example is creating a snapshot named my_lv_snap with a small allocation for changed blocks; mount the snapshot to inspect or copy files as they existed at creation time. Snapshots are not a substitute for backups because they often live on the same physical devices and can fill if too many changes occur. Let's summarize the core ideas to retain. First, LVM is a three-layer system: Physical Volumes are disks or partitions, Volume Groups pool those PVs, and Logical Volumes are the flexible containers you format and mount. Second, most LVM tasks are simple sequences of commands: use pvcreate to initialize, vgcreate or vgextend to manage pools, lvcreate and lvextend to allocate and grow logical devices, and format and mount to make them usable. Third, safety is paramount: always verify with pvs, vgs, lvs and df, shrink the filesystem before reducing an LV, and remember that XFS cannot be shrunk without recreation or migration. Snapshots provide quick point-in-time copies but consume space for changed blocks and are not a full backup strategy. Keep these core concepts top of mind when you plan storage operations on live servers.
